rulesetReview.currentText: Races up to and including 400 m use a crouch start with starting blocks. In most World Athletics competitions, an athlete responsible for a false start is disqualified.
rulesetReview.correctedText: In races up to and including 400 m (and the first leg of 4x200 m, medley relay and 4x400 m) a crouch start from starting blocks is compulsory; longer races use a standing start with only 'On your marks'. Except in combined events, any athlete responsible for a false start is disqualified; in combined events the first false start brings a warning and any further one by that athlete is a disqualification.
rulesetReview.note: PROVISIONAL: sources not opened (worldathletics.org blocked). 'In most competitions' is vague; the combined-events exception is the actual WA distinction. National/age-group rules (e.g. some youth or masters meets) may differ.

rulesetReview.currentText: Races up to 400 m are run entirely in lanes. In the 800 m, athletes run in lanes until the break line after the first bend.
rulesetReview.note: Consistent with excerpts (800 m in lanes to the near edge of the breakline; TR 17.5 covers leaving lane before breakline). Since 2021 one-off minor lane-line touches on bends may be tolerated if no advantage; repeats by same athlete/team lead to DQ (TR 17.3-17.4). Not opened.

rulesetReview.currentText: The baton must be carried in the hand and passed within the designated takeover zone. A dropped baton must be recovered by the athlete who dropped it.
rulesetReview.note: Consistent with excerpts. Change effective 1 Nov 2025 (per press reports): the athlete no longer has to return to the exact drop point; they may leave the lane to recover it provided distance is not shortened and no one is impeded. Takeover-zone lengths could not be verified.

rulesetReview.currentText: Athletes must follow the designated course. Shortening the course leads to disqualification.
rulesetReview.note: Consistent with older rule text and WA DQ list: leaving the marked course and shortening the distance = DQ; also taking refreshments outside official stations is an infringement. Not opened.

rulesetReview.currentText: Walkers must have no visible loss of contact with the ground, and the advancing leg must be straightened from first contact until the vertical upright position.
rulesetReview.note: Matches excerpted TR 54.2 text ('visible to the human eye'); judges issue red cards, three from different judges = DQ (older extract; penalty-zone procedure in current rules not verified).

newRulePoints.text: In sprint starts, at 'On your marks' athletes settle behind the line with both hands and at least one knee on the ground and both feet on the block plates; at 'Set' they rise at once to their final position. (Provisional.)

Since 1 Nov 2024 track spikes are limited to a 20 mm sole (stack height) and road shoes to 40 mm. Shoes must be approved and on the open market before use; non-compliant results may not be ratified. (Provisional - press sources only.)

Athletes may take refreshments only at official stations; collecting them elsewhere is an infringement. Leaving the course is allowed only with an official's permission and without shortening the distance. (Provisional.)
Road courses are measured along the shortest possible route a runner could take within the permitted part of the road, and may not be shorter than the official distance. (Provisional.)

claims.statement: A randomised trial in novice runners found a graded 13-week programme based on the 10% rule did not reduce injuries compared with a standard 8-week programme (about 21% vs 20% injured).
A 2018 systematic review found only very limited evidence (4 studies) that sudden changes in training load raise running injury risk; it is reasonable but not proven to progress gradually.

In a 5,200-runner GPS cohort, a single run more than about 10% longer than the longest run in the prior 30 days was linked to higher injury risk (hazard rising with bigger spikes), while weekly ACWR and week-to-week change were not clearly linked.

In the DANO-RUN cohort, novices who increased weekly distance by more than 30% over two weeks had more distance-related injuries than those increasing by under 10%. This was an exploratory observational study.
Novices get injured more per hour of running than established runners: pooled rates of about 17.8 vs 7.7 injuries per 1,000 h. Build up exposure cautiously in the first months.

Raising step rate by 5-10% above a runner's preferred rate (same speed) reduced knee energy absorption, and at +10% reduced hip loading; a useful cue against overstriding, though injury reduction itself was not tested.
The 2015 international consensus on exercise-associated hyponatraemia advises drinking according to thirst and avoiding forced over-drinking, which can dangerously dilute blood sodium in long events.
For suspected exertional heat stroke, stopping activity, early recognition and rapid whole-body cooling (cold-water immersion preferred) are essential to survival.

A meta-analysis of 25 RCTs across sports found strength training was the most effective exercise strategy to cut sports injuries, while stretching showed no clear benefit. Running-specific evidence is thinner.

Where there is no pavement, face oncoming traffic, keep close to the edge and cross before sharp right-hand bends (UK). Wear bright clothing by day and reflective items at night; drivers can see reflectives about three times further away.

World Masters Athletics publishes its own Rules of Competition (2026 edition) that follow World Athletics numbering for relays (24), race walking (54) and road races (55) with masters-specific modifications.

safetyReview.currentText: Be visible in low light and run against traffic where there is no pavement.
In heat: run early or late, carry water, slow down.
safetyReview.correctedText: In heat: run early or late, slow down, drink to thirst (don't force fluids), and stop at once if confused, dizzy or nauseous. Suspected heat stroke needs rapid whole-body cooling (cold water immersion) and emergency help.

safetyReview.currentText: Tell someone your route for long or remote runs.
Increase weekly distance gradually — a common rule of thumb is around 10% per week, with an easier week every 3–4 weeks.
safetyReview.correctedText: Increase training gradually, but treat the '10% rule' as a rough guide, not a proven safeguard: a trial found it did not prevent injuries in novices. Evidence suggests avoiding big jumps, e.g. keep any single run within about 10% of your longest run of the past month and avoid weekly increases over ~30%.

safetyReview.currentText: Keep most running easy; limit hard sessions to 1–2 per week.
Replace worn-out shoes and change footwear gradually.
Persistent pain that changes how you run is a reason to stop and get assessed — don't run through it.
